newsitem.title: USA: Clinton thanks supporters, goes to church twice.
newsitem.headline: Clinton thanks supporters, goes to church twice.

text.p: A thankful President Clinton used the last hours before his second term begins to go to church twice and touch base with his supporters on Sunday as he recalled how he overcame his "darkest days".

Washington was in a celebratory mood, with thousands of Democratic faithful and others who came to witness the inauguration on Monday doing a lot of party-hopping, touring monuments and braving frigid temperatures to attend a tent festival on the Mall.

But 24 hours before his second inauguration, Clinton seemed focused on spiritual renewal and remembering how far he had come from two years ago, when many pundits thought the election of a Republican-majority Congress signalled he would be limited to one term in the White House.

"I actually, in the darkest days of 1994 and '95, always believed that we would be doing this on this day," Clinton told a Sunday brunch meeting of the Democratic National Committee at a Washington hotel.

"I've run my last race, but we haven't done all the work we need to do for our country, for the 21st century. We have to maintain both a commitment to progress and a commitment to community," Clinton said.

These days Clinton's public approval ratings are soaring above the 60 percent mark. But he also faces numerous investigations into his business, political and private affairs which could sour his second term.

Clinton will take the oath of office at noon (1700 GMT) on Monday on the steps of the U.S. Capitol, the 53rd time the ceremony has been enacted. White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the president was still working on the speech he will deliver to an expectant nation.

The president seemed impressed by the crowds that turned out for the festival, "An American Journey," on the Mall of Washington monuments over the weekend despite the icy weather, which made them rush from tent to tent like students changing classes at a makeshift college in the far north.

"I see the pictures of all the thousands and thousands of people in the shivering cold who were out on the Mall yesterday, all the children taking in the exhibits, and sensed the freedom and the feeling and the enthusiasm in the streets -- maybe this will be better the second time around," he told the Democratic National Committee gathering.
Clinton's wife Hillary also spoke on Sunday to a gathering of Democrats known as "Emily's List," a grassroots organisation of donors that raise money for women candidates.

Mrs Clinton said she thought some of the issues that featured in Clinton's second campaign for the presidency, such as family leave, gun control and curfews for teenagers, signalled not the "feminization" of politics but the "humanization" of politics.

On Sunday morning the Clintons attended two church services. First they went to Columbia Baptist church, where the pastor from Clinton's home church in Arkansas, Rex Horne, was guest speaker. Later they visited the church they regularly attend, Foundry United Methodist Church.

At the second service the Clintons heard minister J. Philip Wogaman remind parishoners that the "one who is called to lead the United States of America" is "not as young as four years ago" and needed their prayers.
The Clintons and daughter Chelsea left the White House late on Sunday to attend a star-studded Presidential Gala with Vice President Al Gore and his wife Tipper.
